Imagine you are buying a new graphics card, or GPU, to run large language models or image generators locally on your PC. You’ve likely seen specs like VRAM, clock speeds, and memory bandwidth, but there is another critical factor that determines whether your new rig can actually handle the heavy lifting of AI: quantization. Think of quantization as a way to compress the brain of an AI model so it fits into your computer’s memory without losing too much of its intelligence. When developers train these massive models, they use a high-precision format, often called FP16 or FP32, which is like storing every single detail of a high-resolution 4K video. This format is incredibly accurate but also massive, requiring terabytes of memory to store and process. For a consumer gaming GPU, even a high-end one with 24GB of VRAM, this is often impossible. That is where quantization comes in. It reduces the precision of the numbers the AI uses to make decisions. Instead of using 16 or 32 bits to represent each weight in the model, quantization might drop that down to 8 bits, 4 bits, or even 3 bits. It is similar to converting a lossless audio file into a compressed MP3. You are throwing away some of the finer details to make the file smaller and faster to play. In the context of your GPU, this means a model that would normally require 80GB of VRAM can be squeezed down to fit into your 16GB or 24GB card.

However, there is a trade-off, much like the difference between a high-bitrate MP3 and a low-bitrate one. If you quantize too aggressively, the AI starts to "hallucinate" or produce nonsensical answers because it has lost too much of the subtle nuances it learned during training. This is why you will see terms like Q4, Q5, or Q8 in AI communities. Q8 is very close to the original quality but still saves significant space, while Q4 is much smaller and faster but might occasionally stumble on complex logic. For a gamer buying their first AI-capable GPU, understanding this balance is key. You don’t just need a card with a lot of VRAM; you need a card that can efficiently process these compressed models. import time
from collections import OrderedDict
from typing import Any, Callable, Hashable, Optional, TypeVar

    entry can have an individual time-to-live (TTL). Expired entries are
    automatically removed upon access or when the cache is full.
    """

            default_ttl: Default time-to-live in seconds for entries.
                         If None, entries do not expire by default.
        """

        self._default_ttl = default_ttl
        self._cache: OrderedDict[Hashable, tuple[Any, float]] = OrderedDict()
